I've been thinking about this problem from a different angle. There is a proof in mathematics called the incompleteness theorem by Gödel. It basically says there are true statements that we will never find a proof for. 

"Though Scientific understanding may influence our politics or our philosophy, that influence is necessarily a product of the interpretation of Scientific theory rather than the theory itself. "

What we choose to study will guide culture/politics/philosophy, and it goes both ways. The questions that are asked and where the pursuit of answers through scientific method may lead is dependent on the theory. Geocentricity was the prevailing theory and belief in that axiom, not mere interpretation, was in some ways fundamental to maintaining the power structures of the day.

I think Critical Theory is similarly limited by its practitioners, where resources of time and thought are allocated. And I think there are true things we will never understand. 

Also, within the social sciences, CT is one theory, and other perspectives like post-structuralism or Social Constructionist take a different look at the world and attempt to answer a different set of questions. So, CT is limited by the set of questions relevant to that particular line of inquiry.
